Aims & Values
At King's Bruton, our values shape every aspect of school life. They influence how we learn, how we lead, how we support one another and the kind of people we aspire to become. Rooted in over 500 years of heritage yet firmly focused on the future, they create a community where every pupil feels a genuine sense of belonging, is encouraged to aim high, and is inspired to make a positive difference in the world.
Aims of the School
The main aims of the strategic development plan are:
School Values
These school values are outlined every year by the School Prefects. They are the values that the Prefects want upheld by the rest of the King’s community. As a school community we aspire to uphold:
A sense of belonging
In a small school like King’s, the community spirit is what makes us stand out from the rest. We are a close-knit school so no one is left out. The friendly atmosphere allows individual personalities to develop.
Ambition without limits
Our size does not hold us back. We have the willingness and determination to go the extra mile and to achieve the best of our abilities both inside and outside the classroom.
Modesty in victory & gracious in defeat
At King’s, we believe encouraging involvement in all areas of school life leads to a more rounded individual. We acknowledge the humility and enthusiasm necessary to do better in the future.
Acceptance and equality
King’s prides itself on the equality and fairness of its pupils. Diversity is accepted and valued equally so no one feels excluded or less important than anyone else.
Loyalty drives life at King’s: this is not only loyalty to friends and staff but also loyalty to Houses, teams and ultimately oneself. Whether it’s on the sports field, or halfway through the toils of the School year, our loyalties will be what inspire us.
We believe King’s shows respect in all aspects of school life; this includes respect towards the School grounds, each other and any member of staff while also being able to enjoy fun and friendly relationships across the age groups.
We feel all members of King’s, staff and pupils alike, are proud to be part of our school community. This leads to a desire to excel in the School and help us to make the School the best it can be.
We both feel very fortunate to have been educated at King's and consider ourselves very lucky to be able to give our children the same education. School facilities move with the times, staff and pupils come and go, but the ethos and culture at King's remains remarkably similar to what we experienced. Our children are very happy and being nurtured in the very best of environments.
Old Brutonian Parents, Duncan and Sophie Weir

Headmaster's Welcome
King’s Bruton is more than a school. It is a thriving community shaped by shared values and a rich heritage stretching back more than 500 years. We are blessed with a wonderful location in the small town of Bruton, and our pupils are lucky to live and learn surrounded by beautiful Somerset countryside.
We are proudly a smaller school, and one that draws its strength from the fact that we combine our size with a truly outstanding education. If you ask our pupils, a common refrain you will hear is how much they appreciate being part of a school that punches above its weight in all we do, offering a breadth and quality of education that you would expect from one many times our size. We do all this, however, while preserving those things that really matter: a sense of community, a recognition that our character is what will enable us to make a difference in the world, and also a belief that school should be fun, with room for children to be children.
Our pupils’ achievements are certainly impressive. In recent years we have had outstanding GCSE, A Level and BTEC results, with the vast majority of our pupils going on to their first choice of university. Our sports teams regularly reach national finals, there are over 70 pupils in our full Choir, our Chapel Choir sing Choral Evensong in regional cathedrals every term, and our 200-seat theatre is the venue for exceptional drama. Our thriving CCF is one of the oldest in the country, whilst over half of our senior pupils undertake Silver and Gold Duke of Edinburgh Awards.
Yet at King’s we celebrate not just our pupils’ achievements, but also the people they become along the way. We aim for our pupils to grow into adults who want to make a difference to the world around them, and who have the character and skills to do so. King’s is exceptional not just because of what we offer our pupils, but because of what we achieve through them. Pupils at King’s are ambitious and confident, but they are also grounded and humble.
It is a tremendous privilege to be Headmaster at King’s, and to be surrounded not just by dedicated and caring staff, but by a body of pupils who are interesting, fun, and kind. It is a thriving school community, and I would be delighted to welcome you for a visit so that you can see it for yourself.
Matt Radley

Welcome to King's Bruton Admissions
A very warm welcome to King’s Bruton.
Our Admissions team is here to make the process of applying for a place for your child as clear, supportive and straightforward as possible.
At King’s, we place great value on building strong relationships with families from the very first enquiry, throughout your child’s time with us, and long after they have left. We understand that choosing a school is a significant investment and an important decision for the whole family, and we are here to guide and support you every step of the way.
King’s Bruton welcomes applications from pupils who are ready to embrace the many opportunities the School offers and who will flourish within our vibrant community. As a largely non‑selective school, we offer places on a first‑come, first‑served basis, so we encourage early applications wherever possible.
Whether you are just starting to explore your options or are ready to begin your application, our team is always happy to help—whether that means answering questions, offering advice, or helping you get a true sense of life at King’s.
We are also mindful that some families, due to changing circumstances, may need to consider a move at short notice. To support this, we offer a Fast‑Tracked Admissions Process, designed to provide clarity and reassurance at what can be a challenging time.
We look forward to hearing from you.
Arrange a visit
Families are warmly invited to visit the School at any time, to gain the clearest sense of life at King’s, we recommend arranging a visit around two years before your intended point of entry. We look forward to hearing from you!
A visit will take around two hours and include a tour of the School, a tour of one of the three girls’ or three boys’ houses and an opportunity to spend time with the Headmaster.
Should you wish to meet specific staff (Director of Sport, Director of Music, Deputy Head Sixth Form, Deputy Head Academic etc) this, too, can easily be arranged.
Get In Touch
To arrange a visit and for all enquiries, please contact Emma Halford-Macleod, Head of Admissions.
Telephone: 01749 814251

We are delighted that King’s has a review in The Good Schools Guide, and feel that the GSG review captures what makes King’s Bruton such a successful and popular school. We concur with their conclusion that King’s is an historical bastion of a school that is absolutely booming in the 21st century.

Welcome to Sixth Form
A Time to Look Forward
Joining the Sixth Form at King's Bruton marks the beginning of an exciting new chapter. More than simply the final stage of school, it is the point at which pupils begin to shape what comes next. It is a time to build on everything achieved so far, develop greater independence and confidence, and kick-start the next vital stage of their educational journey.
The Sixth Form acts as a bridge between school and the wider world. Whether pupils aspire to university, apprenticeships, professional training or emerging career pathways, these two years provide the knowledge, skills and experiences that will help them take their next steps with confidence. At King's, we are committed to ensuring that every pupil leaves us not only with excellent qualifications, but also with the character, resilience and self-belief to thrive in the opportunities ahead.
A Time to Raise Aspirations
The Sixth Form is a unique opportunity to look beyond the horizon and think boldly about the future. It is a time to challenge yourself, embrace new opportunities and begin laying the foundations for life beyond King's.
Aspirational with their time
The Sixth Form years are full of opportunity. Through leadership positions, sport, creative pursuits, volunteering, enrichment programmes and co-curricular activities, pupils develop the confidence, skills and experiences that will stay with them long after they leave King's.
Aspirational in their academic studies
Whatever their starting point, pupils are encouraged and supported to achieve their very best. Expert teaching, small class sizes and a broad range of courses allow every individual to follow a pathway that inspires them, stretches their abilities and opens doors for the future.
Aspirational for their future
As pupils prepare to take their next steps, they benefit from personalised guidance and support, helping them explore the full range of opportunities available. From Oxbridge and Russell Group universities to specialist colleges, degree apprenticeships and professional careers, every pupil is encouraged to find the pathway that best matches their talents, interests and ambitions.
The Sixth Form at King's is where futures begin to take shape. It is a time to raise ambitions, broaden horizons and kick-start the journey towards the next exciting stage of education, training and life beyond school.
King's Bruton has offered both my girls every opportunity to excel and enjoy their time at school. Its warm and supportive environment has provided them with a comfortable confidence within themselves and a knowledge of what they are capable of. As parents we have always had utter confidence in the School’s ability to focus on the individual child and help them to become the best that they can be.

Welcome to Sixth Form

Drama
Drama is a vibrant part of life at King’s, with the dedicated 200-seat Fitzjames Theatre and Drama Studio providing a professional backdrop to a packed programme of productions, performances and workshops throughout the year.
There is an energetic and highly productive Drama programme for the whole School. Drama is open to everyone at King’s, be it on stage basking in the spotlight, or being part of the vital backstage team responsible for the smooth running of shows.
The main School Production, the Junior Play, House Plays, Sixth Form Plays and Staff Plays are regular features of the Performing Arts’ Calendar; there are opportunities aplenty to be involved and to benefit from the enriching experience of being part of a creative team, working towards a common goal. Many pupils choose to take Trinity College London tuition to supplement their training and enhance their enjoyment and success in the dramatic arts.
Drama Scholarships are awarded to pupils who demonstrate exceptional potential in performance or theatre production, together with a genuine passion for the dramatic arts. The assessment process is designed to showcase creativity, confidence and collaborative skills, and includes a monologue or technical presentation, a written review of a recent performance, participation in a dynamic workshop, and a meeting with the Headmaster. At King’s, Drama Scholars benefit from a wealth of opportunities to develop their talents, both on and off the stage, building their performance skills, stagecraft, confidence and creative thinking through a rich programme of productions, workshops and performances.
Learn more about Scholarships and Bursaries at King's

Music
Music plays a vital part in the life of King’s. As a result of the breadth and quality of music on offer, it is not uncommon for pupils to achieve several Grade 8s and a Diploma over their time at King’s. We have a team of dedicated peripatetic specialists to teach, support and guide pupils in their progress. The Chapel Choir sing Choral Evensong at various regional cathedrals each term.
Music Facilities
Ensembles and Activities
There is exceptional breadth and quality on offer for pupils at King’s, with musicians of all levels encouraged to perform regularly and develop their confidence as performers. With over 25 public performances each year, alongside a wide range of choirs and instrumental ensembles rehearsing weekly, there are opportunities for every pupil, whatever their level of experience.
The Queen Elizabeth Music School is a vibrant hub of musical life, alive with lessons, rehearsals and private practice throughout the day. A warm and supportive atmosphere is carefully nurtured, and the constant flow of musicians through the building gives the department its distinctive character.
Music Scholarships
Generous Music Scholarships are awarded each year in January, at both 3rd Form and Sixth Form entry level, to those for whom music is their passion. Candidates can meet the Director of Music informally during the previous term for a pre-audition and to discuss the responsibilities and expectations of being a Music Scholar. More information concerning Scholarships may be obtained from the Admissions Team.
Candidates for 3rd Form entry should normally have at least Grade V on their first instrument/voice and be able to offer ability in a second musical area. Candidates for Sixth Form entry should have at least Grade VII on their first instrument/voice.
We would love to welcome all prospective pupils to visit and see music at King’s for themselves. This video provides an outline of music at King's.

Careers
At King’s Bruton we aim for all pupils to leave school armed the necessary knowledge and advice needed to make decisions about further education and the world of work.
Careers Curriculum
We deliver Careers through the PSHEE programme and this is designed to help our pupils develop the skills and awareness needed for Sixth Form and beyond.
Pupils complete Morrisby profiling at the end of 4th Form with a one-to-one discussion in 5th Form and they can ask for advice at any point. Pupils are introduced to Unifrog in 3rd Form and this is used throughout a pupils time at King’s. In addition our Careers Policy follows the Gatsby Benchmarks and we aim to link curriculum learning to careers in addition to ensuring that all pupils have a meaningful encounter with employers/employees in the summer term of 4th Form.
Beyond the Sixth Form
Careers Curriculum
Gatsby Benchmark Targeted
Pupils need to to define what a ‘career’ is.
Pupils need to discover the Unifrog tool.
Pupils can learn about transferable skills and identify their interests and abilities and how that may help them choose a future career.
1. Brainstorm how many jobs/careers can you come up with in pairs in two minutes. Then come together, Boggle style cross off. Pupils will watch a clip from Casualty/Holby City and discuss the number of jobs available.
2. Pupils sign up to Uni-frog.
3. Pupils complete interests profile and personality profile.
4. In pairs, pupils research a particular job and report back to rest of the class.
What Makes a Good Leader
Pupils can identify the skills needed for leadership, enterprise and employability.
Pupils identify their strengths and competencies and how to record them.
1.Pupils identify what they think makes a great leader.
2.Pupils watch a TED talk ('Everyday leadership' by Drew Dudley), and record examples of when they have been leaders using the Competencies tool.
3. Finish off the jobs that that the pupils researched in the previous lesson.
Pupils can navigate their way around Unifrog, especially the Careers and Subject Library.
Pupils learn about the different types of employment and career pathways.
1.Pupils should identify their activities and interests then record them on Unifrog.
2. Pupils complete the Subjects Library Treasure Hunt to gain a better understanding of HE options and pathways.
Pupils gain an understanding of the importance of making best GCSE choices and having knowledge before making decisions.
1. Pupils study the scenarios emphasising the need to have more detail when making choices. This can then be likened to selecting their GCSE options.
2. Discuss GCSE options - what are core subjects and which are optional?
3. Go through the sheet on Choosing My Options, pupils will write down what they are thinking of choosing and why.
Pupils will gain an appreciation of the types of jobs available and broaden their horizons about post 16 options and career pathways.
1. Pupils play Careers Top Trumps to recap on the many careers available.
2. Pupils make sure they have completed the Interests, Personality and Work Environments Profile.
3. Pupils check their Favourites List and make sure they have at least two careers they might find interesting and research key facts using Careers Library.
4. Pupils make 2 Top Trumps cards with the same categories as the Top Trumps cards, and use their card in their game.
How to Contact Employers
Pupil start thinking about work experience and how to contact employers.
Pupils find out more about responsibilities in the work place
1. Pupils discuss the skills they need to feel confident when approaching potential work experience and employers.
2. Pupils use the Unifrog Apprenticeships Tool to discover potential placement opportunities and complete Contacting Employers tasks.
3. Pupils log this as a competency on Unifrog.
4. Pupils write down questions they would use if they were interviewing someone about their chosen career.
Pupils gain an awareness of a CV and what makes a good one.
1. Pupils look at a good and bad CV. They visit the Barclays website and ‘Play the Boss’ where pupils have to say whether CVs are good or bad.
2. Pupils start write their CV’s on Unifrog.
3. Compare CV’s with others ,if there is time.
Letters of Application (not all classes will do this)
Pupils start to understand the importance and technique of applying for jobs.
1. Pupils compare two cover letters, highlighting the best one, the reasons why, and how they could further improve the letters.
2. Pupils write their own cover letter for a fake work placement opportunity and upload this to their Lockers once complete.
3. Finish with a game of Careers Top Trumps.
All 4th Form pupils are entered into the Morrisby Careers Profiling Platform and run a profile setup. In the Summer term, there will be breaktime talks by professionals which 4th Form pupils can attend.
Pupils learn about maximising employability and maintaining a work/life balance.
1. Powerpoint on what next.
2. Researching opportunities using Unifrog.
3. CV’s and building these on Unifrog.
4. Worksheet on how to look for and apply for positions.
Assessing and Improving Online Personal Brand
Pupils learn how to manage a positive online presence.
1.Powerpoint and BBC videos on Assessing Personal Presence.
2. Paired work on Assessing Security Settings.
3. Pupils build a Linkedin account.
Pathways - A-Levels & BTECs
Pupils learn about different pathways at King's Bruton post 5th Form and the importance of GCSE grades.
1.Personal Development Questionnaire
2.Pupils complete a review of current subjects
3. Pupils introduced to 6th Form prospectus
Pathways - Apprenticeships
Pupils learn about Apprenticeship Pathways.
1.Pupils complete a ‘ what do you know about apprenticeships’ questionnaire.
2. Pupils select interesting job ‘standards’ from standards list.
3. Pupils watch apprenticeship case study videos.
All pupils have a 10-15 minute interview to discuss their Morrisby profile.

Modern Foreign Languages
International politics, business and tourism all mean that in today’s world, languages are essential.
Modern Foreign Languages Curriculum
We are delighted to offer language learning opportunities to pupils of all abilities, ranging from GCSE to A Level in both French and Spanish. Additionally, Italian is available as an extra-curricular GCSE option for pupils as well as Mandarin Club and we’re hoping to offer that as a GCSE in the future. All pupils in the 3rd Form study either French or Spanish, with the option to pursue both languages - a path strongly encouraged for those who demonstrate exceptional interest and aptitude in modern languages.
To enrich the linguistic experience beyond the classroom, we provide a variety of extra-curricular activities, including a Reading Poetry Evening, celebrations for the European Day of Languages, MFL-themed quizzes, film nights, and academic booster sessions designed to further support and inspire our learners.
We also organise educational trips to French and Spanish speaking regions, offering pupils valuable cultural immersion and a deeper understanding of the diverse societies in which these languages are spoken.
MFL Enrichment
Giving languages an authentic context is very important at King’s and that is why we encourage the use of authentic materials in class as well as offering a diverse range of trips, which in recent years, have included Paris, Lyon, Nice, the Dordogne, Salamanca and Munich.

Performing Arts
Performing Arts provide a valuable part of the education and enrichment at King’s. Performers work with outstanding teachers and practitioners to hone their skills, rehearse pieces and, ultimately, to face the challenge of performances and exams. Drama is both exuberant and rigorous; standards are high and much is expected of those who undertake this testing but fulfilling process.
Performing Arts Curriculum
For well over a decade, the School’s Drama Department has been teaching Drama in the curriculum both at GCSE and in the Sixth Form. In September 2019, BTEC Level 3 Nationals in Performing Arts was introduced to the curriculum offering the pupils an excellent opportunity to develop a wide and marketable set of performance skills. It allows pupils to work independently and focus on their strengths, but also to develop an interest in new and exciting performance techniques.
In September 2020, drama was introduced into the curriculum for the 3rd Form for the first time. Focusing on 3 units, the pupils are introduced to terminology, practitioners and explorative strategies that are integral to the GCSE Drama and BTEC Performing Arts courses.
Performing Arts Enrichment
Regular trips to the theatres of Bath, Bristol, Salisbury and London’s West End, both inspire and educate pupils to emulate creative, relevant, highly crafted performances. Regular workshop sessions with visiting practitioners and university lecturers further stretch and challenge pupils to produce high quality work.
Many past pupils have entered the profession to take up careers on stage and screen, and in production support, whilst others have transferred their acquired skills to careers in Medicine, Law, Diplomacy and Journalism. It is a course that will provide you with the skills to progress into the Performing Arts, but equally to successfully progress in public facing careers.
Performing Arts Curriculum
At King’s, we offer the Edexcel GCSE Drama course. The syllabus provides pupils with an opportunity to study both the practical and theoretical aspects of Drama.
However, our GCSE Drama course is not just for people interested in performing or acting. The course is split into three components; Devising, Performing and the Exam Paper. Throughout the two years, you will become a director, a designer, a researcher, a technician and a producer as well as performer. You are examined in three different ways; a portfolio that can written or presented, a performance to a visiting examiner and the written exam paper.
Furthermore, studying Drama at King’s inevitably allows you to develop transferable skills that will be used throughout your life, skills such as:
Edexcel GCSE Drama Specification
Pearson BTEC Level 3 National Performing Arts - Extended Certificate
Our Performing Arts course is for pupils who have a serious interest in developing a wide and marketable range of performance skills. You will study both the theory and practice of a wide range of theatre styles. The course demands practical, creative and communication skills in equal measures. It will provide an opportunity to specialise in different performance genres that you want to develop, and you will be encouraged to find your own artistic voice.
All units are based on practical exploration and skill development but are assessed in a variety of different ways. You will develop skills in performance, critical analysis, research and creativity alongside transferable skills such as teamwork, communication and problem solving. The skills developed in BTEC Performing Arts are transferable not just to those aiming for a career in the arts, but also business, law, medicine, indeed any career which involves teamwork and working with people.
The Performing Arts course consists of practical sessions, lectures, workshops and performances covering a range of skills and include core and specialist elements delivered by subject specialist staff. Listed below are some of the skills you will develop and work on throughout the course:

PSHEE & RSE
PSHEE (Personal Social Health and Economic Education) and RSHE (Relationships, Sex & Health Education) at King’s Bruton, aims to prepare pupils to face the world ahead; they will need to be well equipped to deal with the stresses of modern life, be able to mix with people from all walks of life, and they will also need a global view of a world where boundaries and differences between people are constantly changing.
The delivery of PSHEE is monitored by the Head of PSHEE, the PSHEE Governor, the Deputy Head (Pastoral), Deputy Head (Academic) and Deputy Head (Sixth Form). Pupils’ development in PSHEE is monitored by Tutors through discussion. The content is evaluated by pupil quizzes, questionnaires and teacher feedback.
PSHEE Curriculum
3rd to 5th Form pupils have a dedicated lesson of PSHEE fortnightly where lessons are delivered by teachers with a particular experience, expertise and interest in this area. Tutors are used to support the PSHEE & RSHE programme and some elements are also covered through other areas of the School’s curriculum, e.g. Religion, Science, English and History with 3rd Form.
There are also external lectures for the whole school and three whole school PSHEE days one of which focuses on Relationships. There is a Sixth Form Enrichment Programme focusing upon ‘lifestyle issues’ (drugs, eating disorders, disability, alcohol and sex, managing screen time dependency.)
PSHEE Curriculum
Curriculum design and delivery of PSHEE is split into three separate core themes, although in reality there will always be extensive overlap. PSHEE education addresses both pupils’ direct experience and preparation for their future. The PSHEE curriculum contains a number of elements of statutory Relationships and Sex Education RSE 2023 and Keeping Children safe in Education 2023.

Music Curriculum
Pupils are taught music in a lively and engaging style by passionate and knowledgeable teachers. Pupils are taught to compose in a variety of styles and genres often tailored to their own personal strengths.
The 3rd Form pupils follow an exciting and diverse curriculum that explores how music is embedded in our culture and is used every day to shape and influence our emotions
The course is delivered by performing opportunities, composing, listening or a mixture of all three. Studying music can lead to jobs in the music industry but also in broadcasting, event organising, musical engineering, education and arts administration. Past pupils have gone on to careers in the recording industry, education and performance.

Headmaster's Weekly Reflection
Read on for the Headmaster’s thoughts on the stories and moments that shaped this week.
The October half term always feels particularly well-timed, and the two weeks certainly makes it feel like a proper break. I do hope that you enjoyed time together as families, and that the pupils took the opportunity to relax and recharge. Over half term the local area was, of course, shaken by the devastating news of the sudden closure of Leweston School. This is a tragedy, and the thoughts and prayers of all at King's remain with the children, staff and families who have lost a treasured and cherished school community. A number of former Leweston pupils have joined us here at King's over the course of the week, and we look forward to helping them settle into their new school community, and begin to feel at home. I do want to take a moment to commend our pupil body as a whole, who have shown such warmth and kindness to our new joiners, as well as the staff who have worked tirelessly to support these families in their transition. I very much hope that those who have joined us this week retain fond and happy memories of their time at Leweston, but can also now feel excited about being here, and about what lies ahead.
There has been a lovely energy around the school this week. We have seen trips to Gilcombe Farm for our Food Science GCSE pupils, to Bath University for our linguists, and to Winchester for our Mathematicians, as well as good wins for our 2nd and 3rd XI hockey team vs Clayesmore (playing against their 1st and 2nd XI, respectively), and a hard-fought draw for our footballers vs Dauntsey's. On Thursday evening Blackford hosted a very well-attended charity film night, and the Fitzjames Theatre was packed with pupils enjoying cinema snacks and drinks while they watched the film 'Hunt for the Wilderpeople'. Our charity this term is Good Company Bruton, who do an enormous amount for the local area and its people, including running the town's food bank. Also in support of this charity the Priory girls did a fantastic job selling pumpkins before half term, raising over £1,000, and I am very grateful to the pupils and staff for all they do in general to support our charitable endeavours. It is, of course, crucial that we do so; both to play an active role in our local community, and also to help our pupils understand the importance of being positive contributors to the world around them.
On Thursday and Friday afternoon the campus was also treated to the sight and sound of our military band as they rehearsed ahead of the town's Remembrance Sunday commemoration in which they, and our CCF, play a central role. Symbolically it is so important for the school to come together with the rest of the local community on occasions such as these, and I am pleased that on Sunday morning our pupils will be leading the town procession along with young people from across the community: the band playing alongside their counterparts from Sexey's, and the CCF joined by cadets from Castle Cary ACF. Alongside the civic event we are of course carrying out our own Acts of Remembrance, both on Sunday morning and at 11am next Wednesday, Remembrance Day itself. Since the outbreak of World War One, 119 Old Brutonians have lost their lives in conflict, the most recent in Afghanistan in 2009, and it remains imperative that we remember their sacrifice, and recognise the extraordinary sense of duty shown not just by them, but by the great many who chose, and continue to choose a life of service to their nation. In church on Wednesday afternoon we heard from two pupils with parents currently serving in the military. They spoke of their pride in their parents' service, and about what life is like as a child of a member of the armed services. In a world that remains unsettled and troubled, it served as a powerful reminder of the enduring importance of commemoration and Remembrance, and of giving thanks for those who serve.
Matt Radley

History of King's
On 29th September 1519, King’s School Bruton was signed into life by the Bishop of London, Richard Fitzjames, the Attorney General, Sir John Fitzjames, the Chancellor of St Paul’s Cathedral, John Edmunds and Abbott William Gilbert of Bruton Monastery.
The Founding of the School
On 29th September 1519, in the Chapter House of Bruton Abbey, Richard Fitzjames, John Fitzjames and Dr John Edmondes, three distinguished men who were born in Bruton, granted land and properties to the Abbot, William Gilbert, for the purpose of founding a Free School in Bruton. These endowments included the Manor of Blynfield near Shaftesbury, a share in the Manor of Furneaux in Warminster, and a School House, together with other properties, in Bruton.
The Re-Founding
Following the dissolution of Bruton Abbey in 1539, the School’s endowments fell into the hands of King Henry VIII and the School effectively ceased to exist. After a petition from local citizens, King Edward VI restored the endowments through a Re-Foundation Charter, establishing the Free Grammar School of King Edward VI in Bruton and appointing 12 Governors to oversee its management, creating one of the earliest school governing bodies.
Articles and Regulations
On 6th April 1566, the Governors met and drew up rules and regulations for the guidance of the Governors and the Master. These provided the framework for life in the School for the next 250 years. The School’s fortunes fluctuated throughout these years, with periods of dispute involving the Governors and the Master, and pupil numbers ranged from a high of 50 to lows of single figures.
Michell/Governors Disputes
The relationship between the Governors and the Master did not improve when Edward Michell was appointed Master in 1769, and disputes rumbled on. In 1792 Mr Michell published a pamphlet outlining his complaints, and this acrimonious relationship continued until Mr Michell’s death in 1799. He was succeeded by William Cosens but affairs did not improve, and by the time he was persuaded to retire in 1826, the number of pupils in the School had fallen to four. Indeed, in 1811 there was just one pupil, William Chubb.
Appointment of the Rev’d John Hoskyns-Abrahall
The appointment of the Rev'd John Hoskyns-Abrahall as Master in 1826 marked a turning point for the School. Taking over an institution close to collapse, he revitalised its fortunes through energy and vision, funding significant new buildings himself. During his 38-year headship, the School developed into a respected academic institution, with pupil numbers reaching a record 60 boys and many progressing to university and distinguished careers. He retired in 1864.
The Rev’d D.E. Norton Appointed Headmaster
In 1873, the Rev'd David Evans Norton was elected Master, and early in January 1874 he moved into the newly built Headmaster’s House, which in due course became ‘New House’, a second boarding house for boys, alongside the original Schoolhouse, ‘Old House’. He introduced a welcome stability in the School’s affairs, and he was succeeded by his son, also named David Evans Norton, in 1890.
Plox House Opened as the Junior School
Under the energetic leadership of David Evans Norton (junior), the School developed hugely. A School magazine, titled ‘The Dolphin’, was launched in 1892, and the Old Brutonian Association was formed in 1893. A pavilion was built on Abbey, and in 1902 a Junior School was opened in Plox House, and various facilities - notably Fives courts, swimming bath, and the Wyndham building classrooms - were added to the School estate.
400th Anniversary
A large Hall, with the capacity to accommodate the whole school, together with several classrooms and a library, was planned to celebrate the 400th anniversary of the School’s foundation in 1519 but also to commemorate the 56 Old Brutonians who were killed in the 1st World War. The foundation stone was laid in June 1919.
Opening of Memorial Buildings and Pavilion
It took five years for the Memorial Buildings to be completed, in no small part thanks to James Lyon, an Old Brutonian, whose seemingly endless generosity played a key role in the School’s development over a period of 50 years. Also in that year, the pavilion on Hyde was built, another of James Lyon’s gifts. He had bought Hyde Field in 1914 and overseen its conversion into a fine cricket field, with the first match played on it in 1917.
The Magna Carta
In 1936, while cataloguing the School’s archives, Tom Tremlett, King's Head of History and son of Headmaster Charles Tremlett, discovered a rare 1297 copy of the Magna Carta. Following the School’s 400th anniversary celebrations in 1950, the Governors decided to sell the document to provide much-needed funds, helping to finance the construction of Lyon House, the School’s fourth boarding house. Today, the Magna Carta is held by the Australian Government and remains on public display in Canberra.
War, Austerity and Expansion
Despite many difficulties, the School expanded very substantially during the 2nd World War and the years of austerity that followed, with three new boarding houses, Priory (1943), Lyon (1954) and Blackford (1960), added to accommodate the growth in the number of pupils, from about 130 in the years immediately before the War to about 250 ten years later.
The Junior School moved from Plox House to Hazlegrove
The Junior School in Plox House had been overcrowded for several years, with many of the boarders having to be found accommodation in the Rectory and other private houses in the town. A search for an alternative site for the School was undertaken, and Major Nuttall, a Governor of King’s, offered the lease of Hazlegrove House in Sparkford and this was accepted. The School opened there in September 1947, and since then it has thrived.
Advent of Girls
By the 1960s, the School had grown to over 350 boys at the Senior School, and in 1969 girls were introduced into the School’s 6th Form for the first time, with Wellesley House becoming the first girls’ house in 1984. In 1997 King’s went fully co-educational, with the opening of Arion House for girls from the age of 13.
500th Anniversary and the visit of Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II
In the 21st century, King’s Bruton has gone from strength to strength, especially over the past decade. 2019 saw the 500th Anniversary of the Foundation of the School, and the highlight of this year of celebration was on 28th March when Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II came to open the exceptional, new Queen Elizabeth Music School.
The Sir Peter Squire Pavilion
In 2023, James Lyon’s cricket pavilion on Hyde, built in 1924 and therefore about to celebrate its 100th birthday, and now known as the Sir Peter Squire Pavilion, has been transformed to provide an outstanding venue for hospitality, with a fine extension offering first-class changing facilities. Sir Peter Squire Old Brutonian and father of three further OBs, led a most distinguished career in the RAF before becoming a Governor and Senior Warden at King’s.
500th Celebration
Nearly five hundred years later, the School reached an extraordinary milestone: its quincentenary. Few schools in the south‑west of England can claim such remarkable longevity. In the lead‑up to the anniversary itself, the School marked the occasion with a series of memorable events celebrating its rich history.
One of the most significant moments in the School’s modern history took place on 28 March 2019, when Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II visited to officially open The Queen Elizabeth Music School. It was an unforgettable day for the entire community, perfectly captured in the video linked below.
500th Anniversary Documentary
A documentary film was released on 29 September 2019, exactly 500 years to the day since King’s Bruton was founded. The film traces the School’s history and highlights the major celebrations of our quincentenary year, including the memorable 500th Anniversary Day of Celebration and the Anniversary Ball in June 2019.
Featuring interviews with both former and current Brutonians, alongside extensive archive footage and photographs, the documentary offers a rich and engaging portrait of the School’s past and present. We hope it brings back many fond memories and serves as a fitting tribute to this remarkable community and its enduring legacy.

KSBMotorSport
The thrill and excitement of building a racing car and driving it at Goodwood, Dunsfold Park, Chivenor and Castle Coombe racing circuits. Greenpower Education Trust is a UK based charity which gets young people enthusiastic about science and engineering by challenging them to design, build and race an electric car. King's has two teams: the Junior Team who are in the F24 category and the Senior Team who are in the F24+ category.
